power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Building Research Infrastructure for Meaningful Youth Participation: A Practice-Informed Framework for Participatory Research

author.affiliation:
Department of Pedagogical and Educational Sciences
								Faculty of Behavioural and Social Sciences
								University of Groningen
								
									Groningen
									the Netherlands

text.text: Background: While current frameworks present essential principles for effective youth involvement, they provide limited practical advice on how participation can be organized and maintained throughout research projects.
Meaningful involvement requires not just chances for youth to engage, but also the structural, relational, and procedural conditions that allow them to have real impact.

Objective: This paper intends to present a practice-based framework for developing research infrastructure that enables meaningful youth involvement and to demonstrate its use across the research process.

Methods: Building upon fifteen years of hands-on experience in youth engagement at Jimmy's, we adapt a practice-based ecosystem-based model into a framework for participatory research, guided by equity principles and Lundy's child participation model.

The Youth Resilience Groningen study acts as a practical example to demonstrate how this framework can guide the organization of youth engagement, encompassing the formation of partnerships, defined roles, resources, facilitation, co-design, and decision-making processes.

Results: The framework places equity as its main guiding principle and outlines four interrelated pillars: the research organization, researchers and research personnel, emerging research collaborators, and the broader network of community and research allies.
These pillars are formed through three parallel processes: Doing, Learning, and Organising.

In the Youth Resilience Groningen study, six teens were hired as junior researchers, aided by Jimmy's, and participated in determining research priorities, creating study materials, developing questionnaires, planning recruitment strategies, and developing educational guest lectures for secondary school classes, delivered as a token of appreciation for their participation in the study.
The study demonstrates how organizational structures and continuous support can enable youth participation while addressing ethical, methodological, and institutional limitations.
Conclusion: Effective youth engagement goes beyond just including young individuals in research efforts.
It relies on an ecosystem that allows their insights and viewpoints to guide research choices.
The practice-based framework provides flexible direction for structuring, overseeing, and enhancing meaningful youth participation in research projects.
Youth participation is increasingly recognised as an important component of research (e.g., Rouncefield-Swales et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Youth participation is increasingly recognised as an important component of research (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Rouncefield-Swales et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Young people possess experiential knowledge about their lives, social environments, support needs, and interactions with services that cannot be fully substituted by professional or scientific expertise.

Their involvement may increase the relevance of research questions, improve the comprehensibility of study materials and instruments, reveal assumptions held by adult researchers and strengthen the practical usefulness of research findings.
Furthermore, involving young people in decisions that concern them is increasingly regarded as an ethical principle rather than merely a methodological preference.
Multiple models and frameworks have been developed to conceptualise youth participation.

For example, the ten principles of the European Citizen Science Association's (ECSA) that emphasise youths' active involvement in scientific work, the production of genuine scientific outcomes, mutual benefit, feedback, acknowledgement, evaluation and transparent access to results; Hart's ladder that describes eight levels of youth participation, ranging from nonparticipation to youth-initiated decision-making shared with adults (Hart 1992); and Shier's pathways to participation, (Shier 2001).
text.formatted: For example, the ten principles of the European Citizen Science Association's (ECSA) that emphasise youths' active involvement in scientific work, the production of genuine scientific outcomes, mutual benefit, feedback, acknowledgement, evaluation and transparent access to results; Hart's ladder that describes eight levels of youth participation, ranging from nonparticipation to youth-initiated decision-making shared with adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Hart 1992</ref>); and Shier's pathways to participation, <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Shier 2001</ref>).

text.text: In all these models, meaningful participation is described in terms of what young people do.
For example, they advise, co-create, are involved in data-collecting, help in interpreting findings or communicating the results.
Less attention is paid to the conditions that enable them to perform these roles, or how such participation can be organised across research projects.

Models that focus on the conditions are for example the typology of youth-adult partnerships each describe conditions under which young people can become influential rather than merely be consulted (Wong, Zimmerman & Parker 2010) and the Lundy's Model of Child Participation (Lundy 2007).
text.formatted: Models that focus on the conditions are for example the typology of youth-adult partnerships each describe conditions under which young people can become influential rather than merely be consulted <ref type="bibr">(Wong, Zimmerman & Parker 2010)</ref> and the Lundy's Model of Child Participation <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Lundy 2007)</ref>.

text.text: In particular Lundy's model of space (creating safe and inclusive spaces for young people to participate); voice (information and support to enable them express their views); audience (making sure their perspectives are heard by relevant parties such as decision-makers); and influence (helping their voices to have influence and inform decision-making processes) seems to resonate in Europe as a useful framework for creating conditions by which youth can contribute on a more equal level to adult experts, and for moving their involvement from sec consultation to meaningful involvement (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: In particular Lundy's model of space (creating safe and inclusive spaces for young people to participate); voice (information and support to enable them express their views); audience (making sure their perspectives are heard by relevant parties such as decision-makers); and influence (helping their voices to have influence and inform decision-making processes) seems to resonate in Europe as a useful framework for creating conditions by which youth can contribute on a more equal level to adult experts, and for moving their involvement from sec consultation to meaningful involvement (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Youth participation often takes place within organisations that were not originally designed for that.

Knowing and acknowledging that youth should have a 'voice' does not automatically guide a research team on how to recruit such youth, distribute decision-making authority, budget for their participation, manage possible disagreements, or maintain a healthy collaboration over time (Turuba et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Knowing and acknowledging that youth should have a 'voice' does not automatically guide a research team on how to recruit such youth, distribute decision-making authority, budget for their participation, manage possible disagreements, or maintain a healthy collaboration over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Turuba et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, university contracts, ethical procedures, funding arrangements and publication conventions may also limit the extent to which youth can make decisions, how quickly decisions can be made and which forms of knowledge are formally recognised.
Meaningful youth participation needs more than the mere presence of young people.
It asks for arrangements through which their knowledge can shape the design, questions, decisions, and products of research (Tyl et al., 2026).
text.formatted: It asks for arrangements through which their knowledge can shape the design, questions, decisions, and products of research <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Tyl et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, despite widespread agreement about the value of youth participation, it remains unclear how participation can be embedded structurally in the everyday organisation of research as little empirical work describes this organisational process in sufficient detail.

In the present paper, we therefore present a practice-informed and theory-grounded framework for building research infrastructure for meaningful youth participation together with a detailed description of the application of the framework throughout the research process of the Youth Resilience Groningen study.
This study aimed to investigate young people's psychosocial needs, help-seeking behaviour, experiences with existing facilities and preferences regarding future services.
The findings were intended to support scientific knowledge, regional policy, service development, and the allocation of public resources (for more information, see: https://doi.org/10.34894/WB7YJ5).
text.formatted: The findings were intended to support scientific knowledge, regional policy, service development, and the allocation of public resources (for more information, see: <ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.34894/WB7YJ5">https://doi.org/10.34894/WB7YJ5</ref>).

text.text: The Framework: An Ecosystem for Meaningful Youth Participation in Research 2.1.
Equity as the organising principle
Equity constitutes the central organising principle of the framework.
In participatory research, equity does not imply equal authority or that the participating youth, the researchers, the practitioners and the policymakers should have identical responsibilities.

Researchers are often the ones responsible for scientific integrity, research ethics and FAIR data governance, while policymakers and practitioners or practical organisations operate within their own professional and public mandates.
In turn, youth mostly contribute with their 'lived experience': forms of experiential and contextual knowledge that are not available through scientific or professional expertise alone.

Equitable collaboration therefore concerns whether different forms of knowledge are recognised as legitimate and whether all partners have a genuine opportunity to influence the decisions that are open to influence.
Important to note is that true equity may require uneven forms of support.
A young person who has little experience with research meetings may need a bit more preparation, accessible information or individual guidance, compared to experienced researchers.
Treating both participants identically would not necessarily create equal possibilities for participation.

However, equitable participation also requires researchers to possess the skills and attitudes needed to communicate with young people on an equal footing, recognising and valuing their perspectives and contributions.
Research infrastructure commonly refers to the resources and systems required to conduct research.

In participatory research, this infrastructure also includes arrangements such as relationships, procedures for decision-making, contracts, compensation, facilitation, communication routines, psychological safety, feedback and opportunities for reflection.

Although these elements are less visible than other forms of research output (e.g., the survey), they still help determine whether young people can exercise sustained influence throughout the project.

In other words, the participatory research infrastructure depends on an ecosystem that extends beyond participating young people and its researchers: a network of young people, practitioners, policymakers and other partners who share responsibility for participation.

Based on the progressive insight that the ecosystem is key, and grounded in the theory of Lundy et al (ref), a practice-informed framework for meaningful youth participation was formulated by Jimmy'sfoot_0 .
text.formatted: Based on the progressive insight that the ecosystem is key, and grounded in the theory of <ref type="bibr">Lundy et al (ref)</ref>, a practice-informed framework for meaningful youth participation was formulated by Jimmy's<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> .

text.text: The approach focuses on building an ecosystem for meaningful youth participation, consisting of four interrelated pillars of factors for success.

First, organisational conditions and processes should be arranged to facilitate structural collaboration with young people, including supportive governance, a participatory culture and sustainable working procedures.
Second, professionals need the knowledge, skills and attitudes required to design and facilitate participatory processes and collaborate equitably with young people.

Third, connections with a diverse community of young people should be established, with flexible opportunities and appropriate conditions enabling them to contribute in different ways and at different moments.
Fourth, a network of relevant partners should be developed, supported by clear agreements and appropriate conditions for collaboration.
Translated to the research context, these pillars concern the research organisation, researchers and research staff, young research partners, and the wider network of community and research partners.
The conditions of the ecosystem are developed through three parallel lines of working: Doing, Learning and Organising.

Doing involves working collaboratively with young people, professionals and partners on concrete questions or projects, producing immediate results while gaining practical experience in participatory working.
Learning makes this development explicit through reflection, training, peer learning and coaching.
Organising concerns establishing the organisational conditions, structures and working procedures needed to embed participation sustainably.

Applied to research, these three lines imply that conducting participatory research, developing the competencies of researchers and young people, and establishing supportive institutional arrangements should take place in parallel.

Across these activities, Jimmy's emphasises involving young people from the beginning, taking their knowledge, experiences and ideas seriously, and creating opportunities for different young people to contribute to questions that matter to them.

In the research context, these practicebased commitments can be further specified through principles concerning clarity about influence, accessible communication and feedback, appropriate recognition of contributions, openness to unexpected perspectives and joint reflection.
These principles inform how meaningful collaboration is organised within and across the four ecosystem pillars.
>Applying the Framework Throughout the Research Process
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Applying the Framework Throughout the Research Process</head>

text.text: Young people, youth participation organisations, municipalities, schools and providers of youth walk-in facilities were involved to help ensure that the study addressed questions considered relevant by its intended users and that the research procedures were acceptable and accessible to adolescents.

Rather than establishing one advisory meeting at the end of protocol development, the programme created two partly connected routes for participation: a Youth Core Team and regional network of youth walk-in facilities.
In parallel, representatives of regional youth walk-in facilities participated in consultation meetings coordinated by Jimmy's.

These organisations contributed knowledge about local service provision, young people's encounters with support and the practical conditions under which walk-in facilities operated.The contribution of the regional organisations further ensured that the research questions addressed decisions that were relevant to the implementation of youth walk-in facilities.
The Youth Core Team first contributed to the framing of the research problem and the questions the study should address.

Discussions focused on how young people understand mental wellbeing, when support is needed and which circumstances make a youth walk-in facility approachable or unapproachable.These discussions helped shift the study beyond a general assessment of mental health and resilience, and in the end more attention was given to young people's preferences, support needs, help-seeking intentions and the barriers and facilitators surrounding conversations about mental health.
A Youth Core Team consisting of six adolescents was appointed as a group of junior researchers at the University of Groningen.
Each junior researcher received an appointment of 4 hours per week.

This formal appointment was intended to recognise that participation required time, responsibility and work, and that young people's contributions should therefore not depend solely on voluntary availability.
The young people were consequently involved not as representatives of a target population, but as members of the research team.
They did not participate in the surveys themselves.
Jimmy's occupied a boundary-spanning position between these two routes.
The organisation supported the Youth Core Team in preparing for and participating in research meetings, while simultaneously coordinating input from community organisations and walk-in facilities.
This role was important because the groups used different forms of language and knowledge.

Researchers were familiar with study protocols, measurement instruments and ethical requirements, whereas young people and practitioners more often approached the study through recognisable situations, experiences and practical consequences.
Facilitation therefore involved more than organising meetings.
It included translating between these perspectives while attempting to preserve the substance of each contribution.
Participant information letters and consent forms were reviewed and revised with the Youth Core Team.
Particular attention was paid to length, language, and the distinction between formal completeness and practical comprehensibility.

Information that is legally accurate may still be difficult for an adolescent to understand, particularly when it uses institutional terminology or provides several types of information simultaneously.
Importantly, the aim was not simply to make the materials shorter or more attractive.
The materials also needed to communicate voluntariness, confidentiality, potentially sensitive content and the possibility of discontinuing participation.

Under the guidance of Jimmy's, the Youth Core Team met on a weekly basis and contributed to the research questions, study design (e.g., creating a secondary-education-level guest lecture about research into resilience where the survey was part of), participant information, consent procedures, questionnaire, recruitment and dissemination.

Co-creation was organised as an iterative process in which the Youth Core Team was asked to brainstorm on topics that should be included in the research, materials were developed by the research team, reviewed with young people and community partners, revised and, where necessary, reviewed again.
Their feedback informed project-specific questionnaire items concerning preferences for youth walk-in facilities and barriers and facilitators to help-seeking.
The team also advised on the broader study design, including how participation could be made safe and accessible and how teachers should introduce the research in classroom settings.
Co-creation did not mean that every element of the study was designed from the beginning by all partners.
Some components, including validated psychological measures and formal ethical requirements, imposed boundaries on what could be changed.

The central question was therefore which decisions were open to influence (i.e., being explicit about the influence they could exercise), and how youth and practice knowledge could be incorporated without compromising scientific validity or legal requirements.
In the original Jimmy's approach for organisations such as municipalities, monitoring concerns both the result of the concrete project and the development of the ecosystem for youth participation.
At the start of a collaboration, the intended result is determined together.
During the collaboration, progress is reviewed regularly and adjustments are made where needed.
In parallel, the organisation builds its own ecosystem for youth participation step by step.
At the beginning of the collaboration, Jimmy's and the organisation complete the Jimmy's Participation Scan together.
This shows where the organisation currently stands on the four pillars: people, organisation, young people and partners.
They then determine together which pillars and success factors have the highest priority for the collaboration.
During and at the end of the project, development on the selected pillars is evaluated.
Jimmy's recognises that attention to each pillar is important, but that time and resources are limited.
In participatory research, a similar approach can be used to monitor the development of the research infrastructure.

Researchers, participating youth and partners can examine the starting situation across the four pillars, identify which conditions need attention most and evaluate progress during as well as after the study.

In addition to the development of the conditions, both parties can reflect on whether the participatory youth were able to influence research decisions, how their contributions were used and what could be improved in future collaborations.
Importantly, the four pillars and their related success factors should be understood as a compass for reflection and development, rather than as a rigid set of criteria for evaluating participation.

The model highlights key conditions necessary for meaningful participation but does not specify the exact methods for achieving them or the criteria for determining when they have been adequately fulfilled.

Researchers, the participating youth, and their partners should work together to evaluate how well the success factors have been addressed in their particular situation, and identify any additional steps that might be necessary for improvement.

Throughout implementation, researchers and participating youth should try to regularly reflect on whether the intended collaboration is being realised, which things have influenced decisions and how, and where limitations for participation are experienced.

For example, it is advised for researchers to keep track of which suggestions young people made during the development of research questions, questionnaires or recruitment materials, so that there is a paper trail of which suggestions were used, and which were not. Jacquez and Vaughn (2025) developed the Report of Engagement in Community Research (REACH) tool to document who was involved in which stage of the research, what exactly they contributed and how.
text.formatted: For example, it is advised for researchers to keep track of which suggestions young people made during the development of research questions, questionnaires or recruitment materials, so that there is a paper trail of which suggestions were used, and which were not. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Jacquez and Vaughn (2025)</ref> developed the Report of Engagement in Community Research (REACH) tool to document who was involved in which stage of the research, what exactly they contributed and how.

text.text: Such documentation can also help research teams reflect on how participation was organised and report it more transparently.
When suggestions could not be adopted, to be transparent ideally the reasons should be discussed with the youth.
This is particularly relevant when ethical requirements or methodological considerations limit what can be changed or other decisions play a role where youth might not be aware of.

Young people can also be asked by a neutral party whether they felt able to express different opinions, and whether they feel they had sufficient information to contribute and whether they understand/accept which decisions were open to their influence and which were not.
This way, reflection will concern not only whether young people participated, but also what happened with their contributions.

This is also in line with best practice, as others have also called for creating opportunities for feedback and joint interpretation throughout the research process, including discussion of how participants' contributions have informed research decisions and findings (ECSA, 2015; Staniszewska et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This is also in line with best practice, as others have also called for creating opportunities for feedback and joint interpretation throughout the research process, including discussion of how participants' contributions have informed research decisions and findings <ref type="bibr">(ECSA, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Staniszewska et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The last step is giving feedback, and evaluating the participatory research collaboration.
Experiences from these activities can help make changes to the research process and contribute to building skills, establishing procedures, and organizing future participatory research efforts.
Researchers, participatory youth, and their partners can come together to discuss what aspects of the collaboration were effective and what challenges were encountered during participation.

For instance, this could relate to the time given to prepare for meetings, the availability of research resources, the assistance offered to young individuals, or the manner in which decisions were conveyed.

Based on these shared reflections, researchers, participating youth and partners can jointly identify which arrangements have worked well, where further development is needed and what could be adapted in future projects.

This may involve allocating time and resources to allow young people to take part in research funding, creating more defined steps for working together and receiving input, or enhancing the abilities of researchers to support inclusive and collaborative approaches.

This difference shows the three parallel lines of Doing, Learning and Organising in the original Jimmy's approach: carrying out meaningful activities, developing the knowledge and skills required for collaboration, and establishing organisational conditions that support ongoing participation.

In the context of research, the goal is not only to enhance involvement in a single study but also to build the ability of research teams and their collaborators to effectively support meaningful youth participation in future projects.
>Discussion: Methodological Contributions, Limitations and Transferability
text.formatted: <head n="5." >Discussion: Methodological Contributions, Limitations and Transferability</head>

text.text: The framework does not require the same level of participation in every research activity.

Instead, it encourages researchers to think about how the practical knowledge and/or lived experience of young people can help make the research more relevant, easier to access, and better understood, and what kind of support is necessary to achieve this.
Making these boundaries clear can stop participation from being just a formality when people are formally involved but not given chances to have real influence (Lundy, 2007).
text.formatted: Making these boundaries clear can stop participation from being just a formality when people are formally involved but not given chances to have real influence <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Lundy, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Most important are the establishment of a common objective, the allocation of functions and impact, the provision of support and necessary resources, the organization of communication and feedback, and the creation of opportunities to learn and revise the partnership.
In doing so, it becomes clear not only what meaningful youth participation entails, but also the infrastructure through which it can be organised and sustained.
Weakness in one domain may undermine progress in another.
Inviting a diverse youth team has limited value when members do not feel safe to disagree.
Shared decision-making is difficult when young people receive documents too late to prepare.
Appropriate remuneration may recognise participation, but cannot compensate for the absence of influence.
Co-creation did not mean that every element of the study was designed from the beginning by all partners.
Some components, including validated psychological measures and formal ethical requirements, imposed boundaries on what could be changed.

The central question was therefore which decisions were open to influence (i.e., being explicit about the influence they could exercise), and how youth and practice knowledge could be incorporated without compromising scientific validity or legal requirements.
These principles originated from professional practice rather than from a formal scientific evaluation.
In the present project, they were consequently treated as practice-informed propositions that required translation, testing and refinement within a specific research setting.

Furthermore, the translation from professional to research setting was not one-to-one: some principles could be operationalised directly, whereas others were constrained by ethical, methodological or institutional requirements.

Although in this study we focused on a single study as a case study, the framework is not drawing on a single research setting, as Jimmy's has a lot of other research projects where they collaborate with.
So far, the framework itself has undergone systematic evaluation, albeit predominantly by public and professional organisations (e.g., municipality) and not universities or research setting.
Nevertheless, the experience within the Resilient Groningen Study was very positive.
The framework is not designed to be universal.
Local relationships, institutional requirements, resources, and the involvement of young people and organizations determine the nature of participatory arrangements.
Instead, we recognize a group of flexible design guidelines and thoughtful questions for reflection.
Early involvement does not always mean that all research questions are created together at the beginning, especially when funding agreements or scientific goals have already been set in place.

Researchers should clearly state which parts of the problem definition and study design are still open to change, and provide chances for young people and other partners to give their input within these limits (Lundy, 2007; Shier, 2001).
text.formatted: Researchers should clearly state which parts of the problem definition and study design are still open to change, and provide chances for young people and other partners to give their input within these limits <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Lundy, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Shier, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: This framework is based on Jimmy's practice-oriented approach to involving young people and transforms it into a research structure that is organized around four connected pillars.

Doing, Learning and Organising brings together equity, the influence of young people, and institutional conditions, while highlighting the development of participatory practice, skills, and organizational capacity.
Using the concrete example from Youth Resilience Groningen, the framework offers researchers practical advice on how to organise, monitor, and enhance meaningful youth involvement in research.

It can help research teams and participating partners to create a research infrastructure and ecology that enables assessment of the areas where young people can exert influence, the conditions needed to make contributions, and where possibly ethical, methodological or institutional constraints remain.
By applying the framework, research teams can develop the infrastructure needed to support meaningful youth participation.

In line with Doing, Learning, and Organising, this means connecting participation in individual research activities to the building of necessary skills, new relationships, and organisational structures that support continued participation over time.
